1:
Gill treats the renewal of the commission as a necessity rather than a courtesy: it would have been unsafe for the prophet to proceed on the former warrant, and he points to the Israelites who, having refused the land on the spies' report and afterwards repented of it, went up without the word of the Lord and were cut down by the Amalekites. Henry reads the same renewal as the seal of pardon, arguing from human practice that a commission granted to a convicted criminal is equivalent to a remission of his sentence, and that God's making use of a man is the best evidence of his being at peace with him. Calvin presses back to the cause: the recovery of the prophetic office was obtained by no merit whatever, since by flight the prophet had deprived himself of every favour, and the restoration of his dignity and honour is a remarkable proof of grace.

Henry also finds a probation in it. The prophet had deserted his work, had been arrested for it, had received a sentence of death within himself, and had been released on his good behaviour; the renewed word asks him in effect whether he will go now. Where God has afflicted and then delivered, Henry says, the voice to be heard is a summons back to the duty formerly neglected, and God watches whether men mend the particular fault for which they were corrected. Gill observes that the second commission sets before him exactly the discouragements of the first — the size of the place, the number of its inhabitants, its rank as the seat of the greatest monarch on earth — and that these no longer moved him, because he had now another spirit given him, not of fear but of a sound mind. Henry marks the silence: no objection now that the journey was long or the errand invidious.

Keil and Delitzsch fix on the construction that makes the city great to God, that is, great in God's own estimation, and take the remark as pointing forward to the motive for sparing it should its people hear. Calvin asks instead why the greatness is named at this moment, and answers that it was to arm the messenger: the Lord expressly foretold how hard the employment would be, since many undertake an office boldly and fail because the difficulties were not foreseen, and when men meet more hardship than they reckoned on they faint or despond. He puts the sense as a speech — a man unknown, of no rank, a stranger, is sent to denounce ruin not on a few but on a vast multitude, and to carry on a contest with the noblest and most populous city, a region in itself. The greatness that frightened him at first is now set before him so that he may gird himself for the contest.

The voices divide over what the preaching he is bidden to cry actually was. Clarke takes it as the same oracle already given, which the prophet, after what he had felt and seen of the justice and mercy of the Lord, was now prepared to obey. Keil and Delitzsch render the charge forward instead, as a command to proclaim to the city what Jehovah would say to him, and gloss the noun as that which is called out, the proclamation. Clarke dwells on the word itself: the Hebrew answers to the Greek term for a herald, one who makes proclamation with a loud and earnest cry, and such earnestness becomes a ministry dealing with souls asleep in sin and insensible of their state, for the soft-speaking, gentle-toned, unmoved preacher is never likely to awaken anyone. He adds that this is a different thing from noisy, blustering rant, which shows more of disorderly passion than of the Spirit.
3:
Gill and Calvin both read the bare statement that he arose and went as the measure of the change in him. Gill says he was taught by the rod: he did not stop to consult with the flesh but set out at once, rid of the timorous spirit that had possessed him, his afflictions having been sanctified to restore his straying soul; and he takes the errand itself, a delivered man preaching to a heathen people, as a type of the gospel carried to the Gentiles by apostles whose own commission was renewed after they had failed. Calvin measures the same obedience as faith's energy. The prophet had weighed the greatness and pride of the place and seems to have forgotten that he was obscure, alone and unarmed; but he had laid hold of weapons able to destroy all the power of the world, knowing he was sent from above. Most men harden under chastisement and vomit rage against God; this one was subdued by it, having learned in the fish that the issues of death lie in God's hand.

Ellicott pauses on the tense that says the city was great, which seems to imply it no longer existed when the account was written, though he warns that a Hebrew tense is not to be judged by the analogy of modern languages. The phrase he renders literally as a city great to God, equivalent to divinely great and probably taken from popular speech, comparable to the Arabic idiom that ascribes a thing to Allah, and paralleled in the poetic forms that speak of mountains of God and cedars of God. On the three days' journey he reports a division: one critic takes it for the diameter, while most refer it to the circumference. Clarke settles on the circuit, citing the geographers that it was much larger than Babylon, and reckoning it at the lowest computation fifty-four or sixty English miles round.

Clarke supposes the three days were spent walking the walls and announcing the message from them; Gill and Calvin picture a man walking into the streets instead. Gill notes that he did not turn into an inn to refresh himself after a wearisome journey, nor spend time gazing at the structure and curiosities of the place, but immediately set about his work, and that before a single day's journey was finished the whole city was alarmed. Calvin draws the same inference from the promptness: a man still timid would have inspected the place first, as careful men do, asking the condition of the town, the dispositions of the people, the easiest access and the least dangerous way, and would have waited two or three days before beginning. Ellicott thinks the question whether his course ran straight or circuitous trivial, since the writer means only to convey a general sense of vast size.

Calvin adds that the crying proves courage, since he did not creep in privately as men do when danger is apprehended, and he imagines what the prophet might have thought — that his voice would return into his own throat, that the first man he met would stone him — for he led the Ninevites to no gentle terms but threatened destruction and seemed to offer no hope of pardon. Ellicott hears in the conciseness of the original, yet forty days and the city overthrown, the one deep cry of woe, and compares the single repeated sentence of the great preacher of repentance and the four words written on the wall amid Belshazzar's revelry; simplicity, he says, is always impressive. Clarke defends the number against the ancient versions that read three days, judging that a copyist confused the Greek numerals, and argues that forty days gave room to think, reflect and return, where three would have confounded them with terror and prevented repentance altogether.
5:
Henry calls this a wonder of divine grace and sets it against Israel. To Nineveh God sent one man, a stranger of mean aspect and weak bodily presence after so long a journey, who preached a single sermon, worked no sign to confirm it, gave no directions how to repent and no encouragement to hope for mercy if they did — and they repented. To Israel he sent many prophets, mighty in word and deed, who chose out words to reason with them, confirmed their message with signs, and drew with cords of a man and bands of love, promising great things if they would turn — and Israel persisted. What the Ninevites believed, Henry itemises: that there is one living and true God though they had many, that they were accountable to him, that they had sinned and lay open to his justice, that this notice of ruin came from him, and that being merciful he might yet turn away the wrath if they turned from the sins for which it was threatened.

Gill renders the phrase believed in God, and takes it that they believed the word spoken was not the word of man but of God, faith coming by hearing, which he calls the spring of true repentance and the root of all good works. Ellicott hears an implied contrast to the dulness of those who were slow to believe warnings addressed to themselves. Calvin argues from the phrase to the content of the sermon: since to believe God is to credit what he declares, the preaching cannot have been so concise as the one recorded cry. The prophet must have opened by declaring himself God's herald, or their faith would have had no object; and he must have set their guilt before them as well as their punishment, for had he spoken of punishment only they could not but have rebelled furiously, whereas by convicting them he brought them to own the sentence just and so prepared them for humility.

Gill and Henry both report, and both decline to lean on, a suggestion that the crew of the ship were in the city and told what had happened, so that the deliverance served to confirm the prophet's mission. Gill answers that their faith was the effect of the divine power accompanying the preaching and not owing to the persuasion of men; Henry says only that of this we have no certainty, though he notes that the greater resurrection which that deliverance figured did confirm the gospel of those who afterwards preached repentance and remission to all nations. Calvin, returning to a phrase he had passed over, insists that calling the place a city of God is the ordinary Hebrew way of marking excellence, as men say cedars of God or mountains of God, and rejects as over-refined the notion that it was so named because it was the object of God's particular care.

Clarke observes that they had no doubt the threatening would be executed unless their speedy conversion prevented it, and that although the condition was not expressed they knew it was there, since promises and threatenings addressed to particular men are always conditional, God having been pleased to make them depend on behaviour. Of the fast he says there was never one so general, so deep, or so effectual: men and women, old and young, high and low, and the cattle with them, kept the total abstinence the word implies. Ellicott reads the fast as proclaimed on the spontaneous resolution of the people rather than waiting on authority, and supposes it would have lasted a single day after the Jewish and general Oriental custom.
6:
Gill and Clarke disagree over the throne. Gill will not have it Sardanapalus, that dissolute prince abandoned to his lusts, and takes it rather for Pul, the same who came against Menahem, following Usher; Clarke reports both names, Pul and Sardanapalus his son, but judges it more probable that the monarch was an Assyrian king contemporary with Joash. Gill is struck by the speed: so swiftly did the preaching run through the city, passed from one to another, that in a single day it reached the palace and the royal ear. Ellicott would render the opening not as word came but as the matter reached, and reads the verse as a description of the effect produced on each district of the vast city in succession and on every grade of people, the piercing cry uttered from street to street and square to square arriving at last at the king on his throne of state.

Whether the fast preceded the edict or followed it divides them. Ellicott takes the proclamation of the previous verse as spontaneous, the people acting before authority moved. Calvin denies this outright: it is by no means probable that a fast was proclaimed in the royal city by the mere consent of the people, with the king and his counsellors present, and he prefers to read the earlier verse as the brief summary of the fruit and this one as the fuller explanation of how it came about, the Hebrews commonly relating the chief points in few words and then adding the account. Clarke sides with him in a sentence: it was by the king's decree that the fast was instituted and became general. Calvin also notes a reading which makes the people lead the way and the king afterwards enforce and generalise what they had begun.

Keil and Delitzsch keep to the acts themselves — the king descending from his throne, laying aside the royal robe, covering himself with sackcloth and sitting in ashes — and close with the judgment that however deep the mourning and however sincere the repentance of a people acting on their king's command, this repentance was not a lasting one. Ellicott glosses the robe as the mantle of state, the Hebrew implying amplitude, the same word used of the garment Achan hid; to conceive what the change involved, he says, one should study the descriptions of Assyrian royal magnificence. Gill has the decree carried by heralds sent into the several quarters. Ellicott finds the edict's own form preserved, notes that the term for decree was the technical name for the edicts of Assyrian and Babylonian kings, and takes the joining of the nobles with the autocrat as a custom traceable in the inscriptions.

The cattle detain Ellicott longest. He confines the general word for beast to horses and mules, since herd and flock are named separately, and observes that men think it strange the horses were covered with sackcloth while forgetting that black horses are chosen at the funerals of the rich and clothed in black velvet; the historians preserve instances in which horses and mules were joined with human beings in the signs of public mourning. The instinct underlying the custom he calls a true one, since the destinies of the animals that serve man are often identical with his own and there is a natural bond of sympathy between them, a truth this book gives unusual prominence. But he thinks superstition exaggerated it here, adding to that true feeling the hope that the sufferings of the beasts would help to appease the wrath of God.
8:
Gill and Clarke both explain the sackcloth on the animals by later custom and older poetry. Gill has the rich trappings stripped from horses and camels and sackcloth put on in their place, for the greater solemnity of the mourning, as at the funerals of great persons the horses that draw the hearse are covered with black velvet and others led clothed in the same way. Clarke says the point was that every object they beheld should deepen the impression already made and set them mourning after a godly sort, and he brings in the Latin poet twice: the mourning for Caesar, when the herds would neither drink at the river nor touch the grass, and the funeral procession in which the warrior horse walks stripped of his ornaments with great tears wetting his face. Ellicott presses past the outward signs to the clause that requires each man to turn from his evil way, and notes that the violence named beside it is the trait of Assyrian manners the prophets mention most often, a charge the cuneiform inscriptions abundantly illustrate.

On the king's question the readings part. Gill reports that the ancient versions prefix a word of saying and make it the speech of the people rather than of the king, which he thinks plainly wrong, and that some rabbinic interpreters attach the phrase to what follows, so that it is he who knows the ways of repentance, that will return. Clarke reads it simply as a peradventure left open for salvation: while there is life there is hope, God has no pleasure in the death of sinners, and he has himself prescribed the repentance he waits for. Calvin insists the sentence is a question and not a statement, and finds in it a king who is doubtful but not overwhelmed, still thinking of a remedy.

Calvin then raises the objection against himself. If the king spoke doubtfully of God's favour, how was his repentance serious, since doubt looks contrary to faith, and faith and repentance are joined, no one submitting willingly to God who has not first known his goodness and conceived some hope, while a man touched by fear alone shuns God's presence and passes into despair and hardness. His answer is that there is a measure of doubt consistent with faith, which does not reject the promise but is hindered by other things: a man cast down by fear and then given courage by the hope of pardon is not at once freed from all fear, but while he looks on his sins he vacillates and fluctuates. Two obstacles kept this king from apprehending mercy at once — the express and comfortless sentence of forty days, and the consciousness of his own guilt.

Gill will not let the works God saw be the outward ones. Not the sackcloth and the ashes and the fasting, he says, but the inward works, faith and repentance, attended with fruits answerable to it in that they forsook their former course of life; and God saw them not with the bare eye of omniscience but so as to like, approve and accept them. Calvin reaches the same restriction by a different route, observing that the text names none of the rites but only their turning from the evil way, so that what God looked on was a real renovation. He guards it at once: the question is not the procuring cause of forgiveness, God was freely pacified, and no satisfaction of theirs compensated for former sins. Clarke draws the plain inference that the purpose was changed and the city saved, so the threatening was conditional. Ellicott ends in candour: being wholly ignorant of the nature of the threatened destruction, we are equally ignorant of the manner in which it was averted, though some inscription may yet come to light.
